newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan sceptics doubt sokaiya will fade away soon.
newsitem.headline: Japan sceptics doubt sokaiya will fade away soon.

text.p: Japanese police are urging companies to cut their long-entrenched ties to "sokaiya" racketeers and politicians are threatening stiffer penalties for those who don't.

But in a country where an organisation which domestic media have dubbed a major sokaiya group has an Internet homepage boasting concern for shareholders' rights and posting tidbits about alleged corporate scandals, sceptics have expressed doubts about whether substantial change will come easily.

"Rondan Doyukai wants to make efforts to protect shareholders' rights," says a greeting on the homepage (www.iijnet.or.jp/rondan/aisatu.html) for the self-styled "study society", which some Japanese newspapers have said is Japan's largest sokaiya group with 40 members holding shares in about 200 listed companies.
A Rondan Doyukai official told Reuters by telephone that the group was keen to protect shareholders' rights, but declined comment on whether members were engaged in illegal activities.

Sokaiya are corporate racketeers who buy shares in companies and try to extort money by threatening to expose dubious business practices. They are sometimes also employed by companies to quash questions from legitimate shareholders at annual meetings.
The groups have a long history in Japan, but they recently came back into the limelight with a high-profile scandal involving payoffs by giant Nomura Securities and Dai-Ichi Kangyo Bank.

On Thursday, Nomura President Juniichi Ujiie admitted allegations by the government's securities watchdog of illegal deals with a sokaiya and pledged at a Finance Ministry hearing to take steps to prevent similar misdeeds in the future.

The ministry held the hearing ahead of its final decision, expected soon, on what administrative penalties it will impose on the brokerage over the scandal, which has led to the indictment of three Nomura officials including former president Hiedo Sakamaki as well as of the company itself.
Prosecutors have arrested 11 former officials from DKB, one of Japan's biggest banks, on suspicion of extending illegal loans to the sokaiya at the heart of the scandal.

The latest scandal saga is unfolding as Tokyo kicks off its "Big Bang" reforms aimed at bringing its financial industry and markets into line with global standards, prompting authorities to take a stern public stance toward the misdeeds and to promise stiffer penalties for future law-breakers.

Experts say the number of sokaiya, who are often linked to organised crime syndicates and sometimes threaten bodily harm to executives who refuse to pay up, has declined to less than a quarter of the estimated 4,800 active at their peak in 1982, just before payoffs to the racketeers were banned.

But eradicating sokaiya altogether will require not only bigger fines and longer jail sentences but also a shift in a corporate management mindset which shuns disclosure and gives short shrift to shareholders' interests.

"Japanese management has tended to pay less heed to the interests of its own shareholders than to the interests of its co-called 'stakeholders' -- its employees, clients and suppliers," Masaya Miyoshi, who for eight years chaired the "Anti-Corporate Racketeers Federation" set up by companies in 1989 under police auspices, told reporters on Thursday.
"This attitude can be said to have helped invite the manipulative manoeuverings of the sokaiya," Miyoshi said.
Miyoshi said he expected changing public attitudes, tougher penalties and management reforms to reduce sokaiya influence in future, but some experts are more sceptical.

"Probably some 500-600 companies are involved with sokaiya and unless they arrest all of their top executives along with the sokaiya, things probably won't really change that much," said Tokuo Sakaguchi, a lawyer and shareholder activist.
